name: Hakhun Tangsa
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 5 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Boro, Krishna. 2017. A Grammar of Hakhun Tangsa. PhD dissertation, University of Oregon, Eugene (chair Scott DeLancey). xxx+622 pp. Open access:https://scholarsbank.uoregon.edu/handle/1794/22739
catalog_locator: §2.5 Stress, p. 63; §2.6 Tone, pp. 64-65; §2.7 The Word in Hakhun, pp. 69-72
catalog_quote: 2.5 Stress. Stress is not contrastive in Hakhun, most probably because one of the correlates of stress, namely pitch, is used for lexical contrast. In terms of enunciation, all syllables in multi-syllabic words are more or less equally enunciated. This may be partly due to the fact that most multi-syllabic words are compounds. Except for a few prefixes and suffixes, most grammatical elements, such as case markers, inflected operators, question particles, hearsay markers, subordinators, and discourse markers are all stressed elements. It is not quite possible to tell just by listening to the pronunciation which elements in a sentence are grammatical and which elements are lexical. Therefore, most grammatical elements are treated as phonologically independent particles in this work. [p. 63] ... 2.6 Tone. Pitch is contrastive in open syllables and syllables with sonorant codas. However, there is no tonal contrast in syllables with stop codas. Contrast is found between a low-pitched tone, a high-pitched tone, and a falling contour. [p. 64] ... One phonological feature which starkly contrasts Hakhun with Bodo is stress. ... In Hakhun, on the other hand, most grammatical elements are more or less equally enunciated as the roots. ... Thus, as far as stress is concerned, these grammatical elements are independent phonological words. [p. 70]
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (652 PDF pages; title page: "A Grammar of Hakhun Tangsa, by Krishna Boro, University of Oregon, June 2017", chair Scott DeLancey). extracted text of p. 93 = printed p. 63 shows heading "2.5 Stress" followed by the quoted passage word for word: "Stress is not contrastive in Hakhun, most probably because one of the correlates of stress, namely pitch, is used for lexical contrast. In terms of enunciation, all syllables in multi-syllabic words are more or less equally enunciated. This may be partly due to the fact that most multi-syllabic words are compounds. Except for a few prefixes and suffixes, most grammatical elements, such as case markers, inflected operators, question particles,…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Hakhun is a tone language (low, high, falling contrast on open and sonorant-final syllables; no contrast on stop-final syllables). Stress is not contrastive and there is no positional word-stress rule: all syllables of a polysyllabic (mostly compound) word are enunciated about equally. The only prominence asymmetry is morphological: roots and nearly all grammatical particles are 'stressed' (fully enunciated, treated as independent phonological words), while a small set of affixes (possessive prefixes, class-term prefixes, nominalizing a-, the plural suffix, reciprocal -mun) are unstressed, schwa-reduced and toneless.
new_statements.exceptions: The unstressed affixes listed above; demonstratives, the definite article beʔ/bə and some markers have stressed (full vowel + glottal stop) vs unstressed (reduced schwa) forms (pp. 165-166, 240). Boro contrasts this with Bodo, where the root stands out in loudness and clarity (p. 70).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level, based on the author's fieldwork on Hakhun (Arunachal Pradesh / Sagaing); the text is a general statement about multisyllabic words and sentence-internal grammatical elements, not restricted to citation forms. Van Dam 2023 (p. 94) adds the group-level observation that in Tangsa-Nocte varieties the sesquisyllabic presyllable is toneless and unstressed; the nuclear Nocte (Namsang) tone description in the same thesis (pp. 245-251) makes no stress statement.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted statement describes Hakhun (Hakhun Tangsa), which Glottolog 5.1 files as dialect hakh1236 (under Kuwa) of Nocte Naga noct1238, and which Boro 2017 (pp. 3-4) and van Dam & Rahman 2021 treat as a Nocte-affiliated variety of the Tangsa-Nocte continuum; the speakers are ethnically Tangsa and Boro notes grammatical differences from nuclear Nocte (Haʔva/Namsang/Lowang). No first-hand stress statement was found for nuclear Nocte itself (nucl1786); van Dam 2023 pp. 245-251 describes Namsang Nocte tone without mentioning stress, and offers only the group-level remark (p. 94) that the Tangsa-Nocte presyllable is toneless and unstressed.

tone_statements.citation: van Dam, Kellen Parker. 2025. On the independence of tonogenesis in Patkaian branches. Linguistics of the Tibeto-Burman Area 48(2): 163-192. DOI 10.1075/ltba.25011.dam
tone_statements.quote: The tone system found in the northern branch of Patkaian, also known as Tangsa-Nocte8 is fundamentally a 4-toneme system with surface similarities to that of Middle Chinese, or to the 4-way split of Tai tones9 into A B C and D, where one category is “checked” or “dead”. Across dozens of varieties, the tonemes are cognate … Tone 1 is a reflex of creaky phonation (van Dam 2018: 105f ). … Tone 2 in Tangsa-Nocte derives from words with modal phonation in the proto language … Fourth tone is found only on CVC syllables, and functions as its own toneme
tone_statements.summary: Treats all Tangsa-Nocte varieties as one 4-toneme system from proto phonation: tone 1 *creaky, 2 *modal, 3 *breathy/-h, 4 checked (CVC only); low functional load; pitch values only for Muishaung.

tone_statements.citation: Rahman, Syed Iftiqar. 2016. Verbal Agreement and Grammatical Description of Haʔva Nocte. MA thesis, Payap University, Chiang Mai.
tone_statements.quote: Pitch is contrastive in Nocte. Pitch variation is studied with the help of PRAAT software and also by eliciting tonal minimal sets. There are three tones on open syllables. Open syllables are syllables with vowel or nasal endings. There is only one tone on closed syllables with /p, t, k & ʔ/ in the coda. … Table 7 Tones on open syllables … 1 teeth pa low-falling 134-102 2 snake pu high-falling 184-112 3 sell saŋ mid-level 164-175 Table 8 Tone on closed syllable … 4 tiger saʔ level with glottal constriction 165-163
tone_statements.locator: pp. 15-16, sec. 3.2 Tone, Tables 7-8 (Table 9 minimal sets p. 16)
tone_statements.summary: Pitch is contrastive: three tones on open syllables (low-falling, high-falling, mid-level) plus one level tone on stop-final syllables, with Praat Hz values and minimal sets; called preliminary.

tone_statements.citation: Weidert, Alfons K. 1979. The Sino-Tibetan tonogenetic laryngeal reconstruction theory. Linguistics of the Tibeto-Burman Area 5(1): 49-127. DOI 10.32655/ltba.5.1.03 (sealang archive DOI 10.15144/LTBA-5.1.49)
tone_statements.quote: The tone system of Nocte is of another peculiar nature. It has two ‘clear' tones (low-falling and high-falling, respec- … tively) and in between these two there is a level tone with concomitant glottal stop realization if the syllable stands in final. position; in addition, there is a syllable type with more or less mid level pitch … where the glottal stop is always maintained. … for the tones: /'/ = low tone, f?/ = high tone, /-/ = mid level (with obligatory final glottal stop if the syllable is pronounced in isolated or final position), and /CV?/ = glottal stop syllables.
tone_statements.locator: pp. 84-85, sec. 4 (Evidence for claim 2: Baric / Eastern Baric tone systems)
tone_statements.summary: Nocte has three pitch tones: low and high (both falling glides) and a mid level tone with glottal stop before pause; checked CVʔ syllables have predictable pitch; verb stems alternate low/mid to high.

sources.note: Group-level statement only, §5.1.3 p. 94: Tangsa-Nocte varieties are sesquisyllabic/monosyllabic with lexical tone and 'The presyllable is toneless and unstressed'. §9.3 Namsang Nocte (pp. 245-251, nuclear Nocte, consultant from Phaltan Basti/Joypur, Assam) describes four tones (1 mid level creaky, 2 mid delayed falling, 3 mid level/falling breathy, 4 short checked high) and says nothing about word stress; it quotes Das Gupta 1971's phonology section on tone and dismisses his tone description as impressionistic.
